articles.title: Ganymede Extrait by Marc-Antoine Barrois
articles.excerpt: A darker, louder take on Ganymede: incense, myrrh, immortelle and serious staying power.
body: I finally got around to digging into Ganymede Extrait, the louder sibling of the already loud original, and damn, this thing comes in swinging. People online weren’t exaggerating. This juice is a tank.

I get hit with incense first. Dense. Smoky. Zero subtlety. The mandarin peeks through for a few seconds before it gets buried by myrrh. The immortelle kicks in fast and brings that unmistakable herbal spice. Some people call it curry. I get why. It doesn’t smell like food, but it has that same sharpness that makes your brain go, ok, this is going to be a ride.

The whole thing feels darker than the original. Less spacey. More ritual chamber. You lose the airy mineral sparkle that made Ganymede famous. Instead, you get weight. Heat. Wood that feels almost metallic. It’s not pretty. It’s compelling.

Performance is wild. Two sprays and it clings to your shirt like it paid rent. I get why some people hate it. This is not office friendly. Not MRT friendly. Definitely not lift friendly. Wear this in crowded spaces and you’ll collect dirty looks.
But if you enjoy scents that make a statement, you’ll probably enjoy this one. It has presence. It has attitude. It doesn’t care if you like it. It just sits on your skin and does its thing.
Would I blind buy it? Maybe. But as a spice-and-incense monster with real personality, it hits the brief.
TL;DR: Ganymede Extrait feels like Ganymede after it joined a cult, meditated too long, and decided subtlety is for the weak.

articles.title: The Epiphany of the Clear Skin
articles.excerpt: A reflection on changing tastes in perfumery, the pursuit of longevity, and a longing for transparency, air and artistic restraint.
body: An internal monologue on the natural evolution of art and taste.
For the longest time, I wondered if the fault lay entirely within myself.

I would stand before the sleek, polished marble of the modern counters, surrounded by the newest prestige launches, and feel a profound sense of alienation. I watched people rush to buy the latest Extraits, their faces lit up by the promise of endless longevity and absolute presence, while I felt only a quiet, growing detachment. I asked myself if my nose had simply grown tired, or if I had lost the capacity to be moved by this medium.

But true clarity doesn’t arrive in a flash of anger; it arrives as a quiet epiphany. I finally understand why I can no longer relate to the new world of fragrance. It is not a failure of appreciation. It is a realization of what has happened to the art itself.
We have witnessed a natural, inevitable shift in the cultural tide, a collective mutation of how the world defines beauty.

Perfumery was once an art of the watercolor brush. It was the mastery of transparency, of delicate layers of wet ink bleeding into paper, where the empty space—the air, the evaporation—was just as vital as the pigment itself. To wear a fragrance from the dawn of my journey in 2000 was to participate in a living, breathing transition. You accepted the beautiful transience of the top notes; you watched the composition lift up, evolve, and quietly clear the stage to let your own skin speak.

In that golden era, true art could hide anywhere. You could find a masterpiece of technical restraint—a hyper-realistic, dewy tea rose drifting on a clean green breeze—sitting casually on a lower shelf for the price of a modest dinner. You could spray it without thought, a random mist of pure atmospheric air, confident that the liquid engineering respected your skin.
But a watercolor painting is fragile. It requires an attentive eye to appreciate its shifting nuances.

Naturally, the world sought to capture that beauty and make it permanent. The rise of the clone houses was the inevitable result of that desire—they took the delicate, transparent silhouettes of the masters and rendered them in thick, unyielding acrylic paint. They stripped away the volatile air and replaced it with dense, indestructible blocks of synthetic color that refuse to fade.

The tragedy is not that the clone houses did this; the tragedy is how the world responded. In the rush for efficiency and permanent value, the crowd mistook the heavy density of the copy for an improvement on the original. Loudness was mistaken for quality. Permanence was mistaken for art. Cheap, flat durability was embraced as a collective preference.

And in a market governed by the natural laws of supply and demand, the prestigious houses simply followed the light. They didn't lose their skill; they merely adapted to the new landscape. To survive, they had to lay down their watercolor brushes and pick up the acrylics. They began creating the nuclear mono-notes, the static, unchanging blocks of scent that scream from the first spray until twenty-four hours later, mirroring the exact dense stasis of the clone oils.
Then came the final, corporate stage of the illusion: the theater of the artificial price ceiling.

When the prestigious houses realized the crowd would pay any price for status, they began systematically raiding their own archives. They took those same fleeting, light, watercolor formulas—the casual, everyday citrus-and-tea spritzes that once populated the bottom shelves of discounters—and pulled them from normal hands. They housed them in heavier glass, crowned them with gold-plated caps, called them "Imperial," and slapped a triple-digit luxury premium on the label. They began charging extortionate prices not for rarer raw materials, but for the sheer privilege of breathing air they used to give away for a fraction of the cost.
Seeing this is not a call to destroy the current matrix; it is a moment of profound self-actualization.

I cannot buy these new world fragrances because I am still looking for the water and the air. I refuse to pay a luxury tax for a basic stiletto-shaped clone, or a week's rent for a basic lemon-ceylon tea spritz wrapped in a Roman column. I am looking for the living breath of Antoine Maisondieu’s roses or the floating, luminous steam of Olivier Cresp’s gardens. My home collection is not a hoard of old bottles; it is a preserved gallery of a lost artistic era.

I don't leave the modern boutiques out of spite. I leave because I have realized that my clear skin doesn't need to be a billboard for an acrylic factory, nor a financing vehicle for a corporate rebranding scheme. I have reached the quiet peace of knowing exactly what I love, and realizing that the world has simply moved on to a different canvas.
